newsitem.title: BELGIUM: WEU offers help in Zaire crisis.
newsitem.headline: WEU offers help in Zaire crisis.

text.p: Western European Union (WEU) foreign and defence ministers said on Tuesday they were willing to provide air and logistics support in a humanitarian aid effort in Africa's troubled Great Lakes region.

At a meeting in the Belgian seaside town of Ostend ministers from the 10-nation defence grouping said the WEU would act if asked to do so formally by European Union ministers meeting next Monday in Brussels.
The WEU, often described as the European Union's fledgling defence arm, links 10 EU members -- all but Austria, Denmark, Sweden, Ireland and Finland, whose ministers were attending as observers.

European External Affairs Commissioner Hans van den Broek told Dutch reporters there were 14,000 tonnes of food and medicine already in Uganda and Tanzania that the WEU could airlift to the regions where it was needed.
He also said the WEU was willing to give financial help to African nations that were helping in the Rwanda crisis.
WEU Secretary General Jose Cutileiro would attend a meeting in Stuttgart, Germany on Thursday of countries contributing to the Canadian-led mission to eastern Zaire, van den Broek said.
The Canadian army general in charge of the multinational task force for eastern Zaire, Lt. General Maurice Baril, is also due to attend the talks.
The force's mission grows less clear by the day and Rwanda gave Baril only a low-level welcome to on Tuesday.

No minister turned up, perhaps reflecting Rwanda's view that the U.N.-backed force is no longer needed because 40 per cent of the Rwandan Hutu refugees in Zaire have returned voluntarily since November 15.
The U.N. refugee agency estimates that about 500,000 Hutu refugees have flocked home peacefully since Friday, deciding to quit the war zone in rebel-held eastern Zaire's Goma area.
Rwanda, which denies it is backing the rebels militarily despite much evidence to the contrary gathered by aid workers, diplomats and journalists, says the force is no longer needed.
It wants some of the money for the 10,000-strong force, which has not yet been deployed, to be sent instead to help resettle the Hutu refugees who fled in 1994.

Many countries, such as the United States, Britain and South Africa, were reluctant volunteers in the first place and have seized on the mass migration as a sign that the force should be radically sized down or even scrapped.

But other countries, led by France and Spain, as well as certain aid agencies say the force is still needed to protect and back up a major aid effort still needed in the southern part of eastern Zaire.

If 500,000 Rwandan Hutus have returned that would mean 600,000 are still in Zaire, scattered around a strip 300 km (190 miles) long. Some are known to have walked 200 km (125 miles) westwards, into Zaire's inaccessible interior.
They were caught up in a month-long and three-cornered conflict between the Zairean rebels, refugee Hutu extremists and the Zairean army.

The Hutus fled in 1994 after Tutsi-led rebels won a civil war and took power in Kigali. The political and military leaders of the defeated Hutu regime were mainly based in Zaire, arguing against any repatriation accept by force.
